title: Erdős Problem #461: Distinct Smooth Components in Short Intervals
description: Let $s_t(n)$ be the $t$-smooth component of $n$ and $f(n,t)$ count distinct values of $s_t(m)$ for $m \in \{n+1,\ldots,n+t\}$. Is $f(n,t) \gg t$? Erdős–Graham proved $f(n,t) \gg t/\log t$.

meta.author: Erdős–Graham
originalContributions: Constructive definition of smoothComponent via Nat.factors filtering — not axiomatized
Fully proved infrastructure: list_prod_filter_dvd, prime_dvd_list_prod_mem, no_small_prime_in_complement
Proved smoothComponent_dvd, smoothComponent_smooth, smoothComponent_pos (core properties without sorry)
Proved six boundary cases: smoothComponent_one, smoothComponent_zero, smoothComponent_t_le_one, smoothComponent_prime, smoothDistinctCount_le, smoothDistinctCount_zero
Only sorry: smoothComponent_largest (maximality) — proof strategy documented, infrastructure prepared

overview.historicalContext: This problem originates from Erdős and Graham's 1980 monograph (p.92). They introduced the $t$-smooth component of an integer — the largest divisor whose prime factors are all $< t$ — and asked whether the number of distinct smooth components in a short interval $\{n+1, \ldots, n+t\}$ is linear in $t$. They proved the weaker bound $f(n,t) \gg t/\log t$. The problem connects smooth number theory to short interval statistics, a topic central to analytic number theory.
overview.problemStatement: Define $s_t(n)$ as the largest divisor of $n$ all of whose prime factors are $< t$. Let $f(n,t) = |\{s_t(m) : n < m \leq n+t\}|$. Is $f(n,t) \gg t$ uniformly in $n$?
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization takes a constructive approach: `smoothComponent` is defined via `Nat.factors` filtering (not axiomatized), enabling proved properties. Core theorems `smoothComponent_dvd` ($s_t(n) \mid n$), `smoothComponent_smooth` (all prime factors $< t$), and `smoothComponent_pos` ($s_t(n) > 0$) are all fully proved. The maximality theorem `smoothComponent_largest` remains a `sorry` with documented proof strategy via coprime decomposition. The counting function `smoothDistinctCount` uses `Finset.Icc` and `Finset.image`. The main conjecture `ErdosProblem461` asks for $f(n,t) \geq Ct$, and the known bound $f(n,t) \gg t/\log t$ is axiomatized.
keyInsights: The $t$-smooth component captures the 'smooth part' of an integer — the product of all prime power divisors with primes $< t$
Erdős–Graham proved $f(n,t) \gg t/\log t$, falling short of the conjectured linear bound by a logarithmic factor
The trivial upper bound $f(n,t) \leq t$ is proved; the conjecture asks for $f(n,t) = \Theta(t)$
The formalization is notably strong: most theorems are fully proved, with only the maximality property `smoothComponent_largest` as a sorry
The smooth-rough decomposition $n = s_t(n) \cdot c$ (where all primes of $c$ are $\geq t$) is key infrastructure prepared for the maximality proof

sections.title: Smooth Components
sections.summary: Constructive definition of `smoothComponent` via `Nat.factors` filtering. Includes infrastructure lemmas (`list_prod_filter_dvd`, `prime_dvd_list_prod_mem`, `no_small_prime_in_complement`) and three core proved theorems: $s_t(n) \mid n$, all prime factors $< t$, $s_t(n) > 0$. The maximality theorem `smoothComponent_largest` has `sorry` with a documented coprime decomposition strategy.

sections.title: Counting Distinct Smooth Components
sections.summary: Defines $f(n,t) = |\text{image}(s_t, [n+1, n+t])|$ using `Finset.Icc` and `Finset.image`. Noncomputable since `smoothComponent` involves factorization.

sections.title: Main Conjecture
sections.summary: States `ErdosProblem461`: $\exists C > 0,\, \exists t_0,\, \forall t \geq t_0,\, \forall n,\, f(n,t) \geq Ct$. Quantifies uniformly over all starting points $n$.

sections.title: Known Results
sections.summary: Axiomatizes the Erdős–Graham bound $f(n,t) \geq C \cdot t/\log t$ using `Real.log`. The logarithmic gap between this and the conjectured $Ct$ is the open question.

sections.title: Basic Properties
sections.summary: Six fully proved results: $s_t(1) = 1$, $s_t(0) = 1$, $t \leq 1 \implies s_t(n) = 1$, $s_t(p) = p$ if $p < t$ else $1$, $f(n,t) \leq t$, and $f(n,0) = 0$. All use `Nat.factors` properties and `Finset` cardinality bounds.

conclusion.summary: The formalization of Erdős Problem 461 is notably strong: the smooth component is constructively defined (not axiomatized), and most core properties are fully proved. The only sorry is the maximality theorem, for which the infrastructure (complement lemma, list product divisibility) is already in place. The gap between the known $t/\log t$ bound and the conjectured linear bound remains open.
conclusion.implications: Resolution would reveal fine structure in the distribution of smooth parts of integers across short intervals. The constructive definition and proved properties make this formalization particularly amenable to Aristotle proof search for the remaining sorry.
openQuestions: Is $f(n,t) \gg t$ or is the logarithmic loss in the Erdős–Graham bound essential?
What is the true order of growth of $\min_n f(n,t)$?
Can improved sieve methods or the Hildebrand–Tenenbaum framework close the $\log t$ gap?
Can the maximality theorem `smoothComponent_largest` be proved using the existing infrastructure?
